paragraphs: Here's what I want you to take from Eliphaz, friend. He says a lot of true-sounding things. He says God puts no trust in His holy ones and that even the heavens are not pure in His eyes (Job 15:15). But he points all of it at Job, a man who has just lost his children, his wealth and his health (Job 1:13-19; 2:7).

Look at how he does it. He leans on the gray-haired men on his side, and he says what he has seen and what the wise men passed down (Job 15:10, 17-18). Then he describes a wicked man who suffers all his days (Job 15:20). I think Eliphaz is saying Job must be that man, but he never says so outright. Job's suffering is the thing he's trying to explain, and the Bible hasn't told us that's why it came.

So here's the lesson, baker. Old sayings and a big crowd behind you can make an argument sound solid, but they don't make it fit the person in front of you. Eliphaz started by asking if God's consolations were not enough for Job, "even words spoken gently to you" (Job 15:11). Yet his own words were anything but gentle. When somebody hurts, ask whether your words will comfort them, and keep listening. And this conversation isn't over, so stay with me.
